newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks finish lower as property stocks tumble.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks finish lower as property stocks tumble.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks ended with heavy losses on Wednesday, beaten down by interest rate concerns and a slide in the property sector after recommendations that banks curb lending for luxury property acquisitions.
The Hang Seng Index fell 117.86 points or 0.88 percent to 13,285.43. Turnover was HK$11.89 billion versus Tuesday's HK$8.64 billion.
"Today we were affected by several cross currents," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
"We are watching the long bond which is reaching a high level. The latest move on bank lending is just another negative amid a fair amount of uncertainty in the market right now."
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority recommended on Tuesday that the maximum loan to value ratio for properties worth more than HK$12 million should be reduced to 60 percent from 70 percent.
Shares in Cheung Kong fell HK$2.50 to HK$72.25, while Henderson Land slid HK$2.25 to HK$72.50 and Sun Hung Kai Properties dropped HK$2.00 to HK$88.75.
"We are still concerned about the interest rate trend," said Amy Wong, research director at New China Hong Kong Securities.
"We have the FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting next week so before the meeting people are quite uncertain."
A share deal between CITIC Pacific and China Light & Power failed to buoy the market although it did give share prices a firmer start on Wednesday.
CITIC Pacific said on Tuesday it would take a 20 percent stake in China Light, boosting China Light shares HK$1.10 to HK$34.80 but leaving CITIC Pacific off HK$1.00 at HK$38.50.
Analysts said investors were concerned CITIC would have to issue new shares to fund the HK$16.25 billion acquisition.
"We are still waiting for major plans to be announced," said Wong. "Up to now we see major cash being injected into China Light but we have not heard of any major plans."
Analysts said lingering uncertainty about interest rates was likely to keep stocks in a range over the near term.

"I think we are in no-man's land for the time being. We are sort of feeling out the lower end of what may be a trading range for a while until people are more certain about the direction of interest rates in the U.S.," said Gorges.
January Hang Seng Index futures, which expire on Thursday, fell 140 points to 13,225.
